result: Double-edged TJ polygons exist in murine ear epidermis with regular size and Z-axis positioning. Approximately 9.8% of TJ polygons are double-edged, with outer polygons larger and positioned higher than inner polygons, which are smaller and positioned lower relative to adjacent single-edged polygons.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6 provide quantitative morphometric data from multiple independent assays (n=5 for frequency, n=23-66 for size measurements, n=55-99 for Z-axis positioning) with statistical analysis showing significant differences. The data are internally consistent and supported by 3D imaging evidence in Figures 1B-E.

result: Double-edged polygons represent sites of cell translocation across the TJ barrier. Live imaging shows that a new interior polygon appears beneath a pre-existing exterior polygon, forming a double-edged structure, followed by disappearance of the exterior polygon, enabling cell body translocation from inside to outside the TJ barrier.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by in vivo live imaging data (Figure 1F, Video 4) showing the temporal sequence of polygon appearance and disappearance. Claim C21 is a reasonable inference from the observed dynamics. The evidence directly demonstrates the mechanism of TJ replacement during cell turnover.

result: Interior TJ polygons exhibit functional barrier properties before exterior polygons disappear. The interior polygons protect against ETA permeation, preventing barrier leakage during cellular translocation, with the precise temporal order of TJ formation being critical for barrier homeostasis.
evaluation: Claim C9 is supported by quantitative permeation assay data (n=149 double-edged, n=736 single-edged polygons) showing significantly higher Dsg1-EC protection in double-edged polygons (Figure 2A-D, Video 5). Claims C22 and C41 are reasonable inferences from these data and the observed dynamics. The barrier function is directly demonstrated experimentally.

result: Interior polygons are tricellular TJs (tTJs) while exterior polygons are bicellular TJs (bTJs). tTJ-specific proteins (angulin-1 and tricellulin) localize to all edges of interior polygons, while claudin-1 localizes to both polygon types. Interior polygons consist of tTJs formed among three SG2 cells: two vertically aligned and one laterally adjacent.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 2B, E, Video 6, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) showing distinct localization patterns of TJ proteins. Claim C12 is a structural inference consistent with the observed tTJ protein localization and 3D architecture. The molecular characterization is well-documented.

result: SG2 cells have a flattened Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron (f-TKD) shape with TJs on their edges. This polyhedral shape was previously observed in corneocytes but overlooked, and represents the optimal space-filling shape with minimal surface area originally proposed by Lord Kelvin in 1887.
evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by 3D imaging and rendering of isolated SG2 cells (Figure 3F, Video 7). Claims C43-C44 provide historical context with appropriate citations. The f-TKD shape is directly demonstrated through immunofluorescence and 3D reconstruction, though the claim of 'optimal' shape is based on theoretical considerations rather than experimental proof.

result: A computational model based on three local rules governing f-TKD cells reproduces the entire sequence of TJ replacement, cell turnover, and barrier homeostasis. The model parameters were calibrated to match the observed 9.8% double-edged polygon frequency and 24-hour SG2 turnover time.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by computational simulation results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Videos 9-10) that reproduce observed dynamics. Claim C42 uses an estimate from prior literature (Potten, 1975) for calibration. The model successfully recapitulates experimental observations, though validation is limited to qualitative agreement with the double-edged polygon frequency.

result: The f-TKD model explains the regular zig-zag interdigitation pattern of corneocytes observed in murine ear epidermis and suggests that SC-SG homeostasis is maintained by spatiotemporal orchestration of cell differentiation in the SG2 layer rather than by basal layer kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by prior observations (citations to Mackenzie 1969, 1975; Christophers 1972; Menton 1976; Ball 2001) and computational simulation (Figure 6A). Claims C23 and C26 are inferences from the model's ability to reproduce observed patterns. The model provides a coherent mechanistic explanation, though direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanism is limited.

result: The f-TKD model is consistent with prior computational and experimental studies showing random cell supply from basal/spinous layers and cell funneling into SG columns. Cell columns exist only in SG and SC layers, with tightly coordinated turnover in adjacent columns producing the regular interdigitation pattern.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 appropriately cite prior work (Honda et al. 1996; Doupé et al. 2010; Rompolas et al. 2016) showing consistency with the proposed model. Claims C29-C30 are key features of the f-TKD model supported by the computational simulations and observed interdigitation patterns. The model reconciles previous observations with the new findings.

result: The mammalian epidermis has two physical barriers (SC and TJ), with the TJ barrier consisting of a single honeycomb layer in the SG2 layer. Keratinocytes differentiate sequentially through epidermal layers, and barrier dysfunction causes congenital disorders and allergic disease predisposition.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C15-C20) provide established background knowledge supported by multiple prior citations (Kubo et al. 2012; Furuse et al. 2002; Mackenzie 1969, 1975; and others). The claims accurately represent prior work and provide appropriate context for the current study.

result: TJ formation is restricted to SG2 cells in the epidermis. In simple epithelia, bTJs form between two cells and tTJs at tricellular contacts. Prior permeation assays showed no barrier leakage, suggesting TJ homeostasis is maintained during polygon replacement.
evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E. Claim C45 is supported by prior work (Furuse et al. 2014). Claims C46-C47 appropriately cite prior studies (Furuse et al. 2002; Kubo et al. 2009) and make reasonable inferences about barrier homeostasis.

result: The f-TKD cell turnover mechanism may govern cell differentiation across mammalian species, as various mammalian epidermis shows regular interdigitation patterns. The model provides a fundamental basis for barrier homeostasis in cornified stratified epithelia.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by citations to prior observations (Christophers 1972; Mackenzie et al. 1981) but represent extrapolations beyond the mouse ear epidermis studied here. Claim C37 is a broad concluding inference. Direct experimental validation in other species or tissue types is lacking, making generalizability uncertain.

result: Single-layered TJ barriers are biologically reasonable in stratified epithelia because multi-layered barriers would segregate upper cells from nutrient supply via paracellular pathways from basal connective tissue.
evaluation: Claim C31 is speculative reasoning, but C32 is supported by citations (Kubo et al. 2012; Yoshida et al. 2013) and biological logic. Claim C49 represents established knowledge about nutrient supply. The reasoning is sound though not directly tested experimentally.

result: Epidermal homeostasis involves balancing multiple processes. Alternative mechanisms may maintain TJ homeostasis in simple/non-cornified epithelia. Optimal space-filling shapes may be more complex than Kelvin's model, and human skin shows more variegated corneocyte patterns than mouse ear skin.
evaluation: Claim C48 is a general inference about homeostasis. Claim C50 appropriately cites alternative mechanisms (Pentecost et al. 2006; Eisenhoffer and Rosenblatt 2011). Claims C51-C52 acknowledge limitations with appropriate citations (Lewis 1943; Williams 1968; Weaire and Phelan 1994; Mackenzie et al. 1981). These represent appropriate caveats and context.

result: The epidermal proliferative unit (EPU) concept from the 1980s has been superseded by the epidermal differentiation unit (EDU) concept based on recent cell-fate-tracing studies showing more random cell fate decisions in the basal layer.
evaluation: Both claims appropriately cite prior work (Potten and Allen 1975; Potten 2004 for C53; Rompolas et al. 2016 for C54) and accurately represent the evolution of concepts in the field. This provides important historical and conceptual context.

result: ZO-1-Venus transgenic mice were generated using the involucrin promoter and successfully label TJs without morphological changes or loss of occlusive function. Female 8-12 week-old C57B6/J mice were used as wild type.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 describe methods and validation of the transgenic model. The ZO-1-Venus construct is validated by colocalization with occludin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and functional permeation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). The transgenic model is appropriately characterized.
